strengths: The conditional summary graph is a useful contribution: it represents asynchronous changes in individual variables’ outgoing interactions using K graph templates. This provides a compact, well-motivated extension of the stationary graph representation used by ACD.

The synthetic results demonstrate substantial benefits in several intended settings. For example, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy for SDCI versus 60.45% for ACD in the two-edge-type hidden-state setting. Tables 3–4 also show improvements in graph recovery and reconstruction.

The evaluation spans linear systems, spring interactions, and NBA trajectories, with additional studies of data efficiency and transfer across variable counts and teams. The figures clarify the representation, and the appendices provide substantial simulation and training details.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result needs stronger assumptions and a more complete proof. Theorem 1 omits the nonconstant-mechanism assumption used in Lemma 2. Appendix A.3 then asserts conditional dependence given all previous-time variables, although causal minimality only directly establishes dependence given the other parents; additional support conditions and justification are needed. Furthermore, merely observing an endogenous state sequence does not automatically preserve the conditional Markov property asserted in Lemma 1. The result also concerns population identifiability, rather than a recovery guarantee for the proposed variational estimator.

The comparisons do not adequately establish the advantage over methods designed for changing regimes. ACD assumes a stationary graph, while several other baselines target smooth changes, a mismatch the paper itself acknowledges. Regime-PCMCI, identified as closely related, is not evaluated. A switching or state-conditioned baseline and a dynamic graph predictor trained on the same collection of sequences would better isolate the contribution. Comparisons against methods fitted separately to individual sequences also combine the benefits of state modeling with those of amortized training.

The claimed hidden-state coverage is broader than the demonstrated results. The introduction suggests coverage of scenario classes 1–3, but Appendix F.2 explicitly reports unsuccessful graph recovery with hidden history-dependent states and instead supplies state information. The inference model q(s_i^t | x_i^t) also lacks memory for such states. Even within scenario class 2, conditional-graph accuracy falls from 98.08% in the two-edge-type case to 65.45% in the unrestricted three-edge-type case. Claims should reflect this narrower demonstrated capability.

The synthetic evaluation leaves important robustness questions unresolved. The number of states and edge types is supplied, while linear trajectories are filtered for comparable initial/final magnitudes and approximately balanced state visitation. These choices favor the assumed model and can alter the sampled distribution. Sensitivity to state-count misspecification, rare states, and the trajectory-selection procedure would materially strengthen the evidence.

The NBA experiment supports forecasting utility but does not establish that causal graph recovery explains the improvement. There is no graph ground truth or ablation separating causal structure from a flexible state-dependent graph architecture. A comparable noncausal graph predictor would help. The protocol should also specify whether future ball trajectories are supplied and how games or events are separated between training and testing, so the forecasting results can be interpreted correctly.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix detail. The state-predictor architecture, the role of the otherwise undefined λ in Appendix C.2, baseline threshold selection, and any permutation alignment used to score latent states and edge types need specification. The number of independent runs and meaning of the reported error bars are also unclear. Smaller presentation issues include the unresolved equation reference in Appendix C.1 and inconsistent SDCI/SCDI naming.
